note: Plain-language guide to NASA Earth science variables that can be tested for trends. Product short names and fields come from the NASA product pages; giovanni_id is given only where the team has used or confirmed it, otherwise search Giovanni for the product short name. available_now is filled in by the API from the loaded data.

themes.water: Rain, soil water, evaporation, rivers and groundwater
themes.air: Haze, smoke, pollution gases and ozone
themes.land: Plants, forests, fires and land surface

place_types.city: A large city or industrial area
place_types.mountain_snow: Mountains with seasonal snow or glaciers

variables.name: Precipitation (rain and melted snow)
variables.plain_definition: How much water falls from the sky, measured as a depth, like water collecting in a bucket.
variables.why_trends: Warming changes how much water the air holds and where storms track, so some regions get wetter and others drier.
variables.caveat: Rainfall varies a lot year to year, so trends usually need long records to become significant.

variables.name: Aerosol optical depth (haze)
variables.plain_definition: How much sunlight is blocked by tiny particles such as dust, smoke and pollution in the whole column of air. 0.1 is clear; above 1 is very hazy.
variables.why_trends: Changes in traffic, industry, crop burning, dust storms and wildfires change how many particles are in the air.
variables.caveat: Measured only in clear skies, so cloudy and rainy months have fewer observations. AOD is not the same as ground-level PM2.5.

variables.name: Aerosol optical depth (model reanalysis)
variables.plain_definition: The same haze measure, estimated by NASA's MERRA-2 model, which fills cloudy days by combining observations with physics.
variables.why_trends: Useful as a cross-check on satellite AOD where clouds hide the surface.
variables.caveat: A model product that assimilates observations; it is not independent truth.

variables.name: Nitrogen dioxide (tropospheric column)
variables.plain_definition: A brown gas from burning fuel in cars, power plants and factories, measured as the amount of gas above each square centimetre of ground.
variables.why_trends: Cleaner engines and fuel rules make it fall; fast-growing traffic and industry make it rise. Cities can trend in opposite directions.
variables.caveat: OMI has a 'row anomaly' since 2007 that reduces coverage; the cloud-screened field drops cloudy pixels.

variables.name: Total column ozone
variables.plain_definition: The total amount of ozone in the air above a point, mostly high up in the protective ozone layer, measured in Dobson units.
variables.why_trends: The ozone layer thinned after CFC use and is slowly recovering since the Montreal Protocol.
variables.caveat: Recovery is slow; a 20-year record may show only a small change.

variables.name: Sulfur dioxide (planetary boundary layer)
variables.plain_definition: A gas from burning coal and from volcanoes, measured near the ground.
variables.why_trends: Power-plant scrubbers make it drop sharply in some countries while new coal plants raise it elsewhere.
variables.caveat: Noisy outside strong sources; volcanic eruptions make single-month spikes.

variables.name: UV aerosol index (smoke and dust)
variables.plain_definition: A number that is high when light-absorbing smoke or dust is in the air, even above clouds.
variables.why_trends: Wildfire seasons and dust storms change from year to year and can show long-term shifts.
variables.caveat: An index, not a concentration; compare it only with itself.

variables.name: Near-surface air temperature
variables.plain_definition: How warm the air is about 2 metres above the ground, the temperature you would feel.
variables.why_trends: Greenhouse warming raises temperatures nearly everywhere, but by different amounts.
variables.caveat: Kelvin and Celsius differ only by 273.15, so a slope in K per decade equals a slope in degrees C per decade.

variables.name: Surface air temperature from AIRS
variables.plain_definition: The temperature of the air just above the surface, measured by an infrared sounder looking down from space.
variables.why_trends: An observation-based check on model temperature trends.
variables.caveat: Infrared retrievals are less reliable under thick cloud.

variables.name: Total water vapour
variables.plain_definition: All the water held as invisible gas in a column of air, as if it were squeezed out into a layer of liquid.
variables.why_trends: Warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour per degree, so vapour often rises with temperature.
variables.caveat: Cloudy scenes reduce sampling.

variables.name: Land surface temperature (day)
variables.plain_definition: How hot the ground itself is, as seen by a heat camera from space. Roads and roofs get much hotter than parks.
variables.why_trends: Cities growing, forests cleared or deserts spreading make the ground hotter; irrigation can cool it.
variables.caveat: Only cloud-free days; different from air temperature.

variables.name: Vegetation greenness (NDVI)
variables.plain_definition: A score from -1 to 1 for how green and leafy the land is. Dense forest is about 0.8, bare desert near 0.1.
variables.why_trends: Deforestation, farming, drought and longer growing seasons change how green the land is.
variables.caveat: Greener is not always healthier: irrigated crops can raise NDVI where natural forest was lost.

variables.name: Snow cover
variables.plain_definition: The percentage of the ground covered by snow each month.
variables.why_trends: Warmer winters shorten the snow season, which changes river flow and water supply downstream.
variables.caveat: Clouds hide snow; polar night has no data.

variables.name: Soil moisture (top 10 cm)
variables.plain_definition: How wet the top layer of soil is, measured as kilograms of water in each square metre.
variables.why_trends: Less rain, more evaporation or heavy irrigation change how much water stays in the soil, which matters for crops and droughts.
variables.caveat: A model estimate driven by observed rain and weather, not a direct measurement.

variables.name: Evapotranspiration
variables.plain_definition: Water moving from the land into the air by evaporation from soil and water, plus 'sweating' from plant leaves.
variables.why_trends: Warmer air and more irrigation raise it; drought and forest loss can lower it.
variables.caveat: Multiply kg/m2/s by 86400 x days in the month for mm/month.

variables.name: Surface runoff (streamflow source)
variables.plain_definition: Rain and melt water that flows over the ground into streams instead of soaking in.
variables.why_trends: Heavier downpours, paving and snowmelt timing change how much water reaches rivers.
variables.caveat: A model estimate; for real river gauges use CUAHSI HydroShare or national gauge networks.

variables.name: Snow water equivalent
variables.plain_definition: How much water you would get if you melted all the snow on the ground.
variables.why_trends: Mountain snowpacks store water for summer; warming reduces them.
variables.caveat: Model estimate; complex mountain terrain is smoothed at 0.25 degree.

variables.name: Terrestrial water storage (groundwater and all water)
variables.plain_definition: Changes in all the water stored on and under the land, measured by tiny changes in Earth's gravity.
variables.why_trends: Pumping groundwater for farms makes it fall year after year; it is one of the clearest human signals from space.
variables.caveat: There is an 11-month gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO (2017-2018); leave it missing, never fill it.

variables.name: Sea surface temperature
variables.plain_definition: How warm the top layer of the ocean is.
variables.why_trends: The oceans absorb most extra heat from global warming; warmer seas affect coral, fish and storms.
variables.caveat: Skin temperature from clear-sky infrared; clouds reduce sampling.

variables.name: Ocean chlorophyll-a (plankton)
variables.plain_definition: How much green plankton is in surface water, the base of the ocean food chain.
variables.why_trends: River nutrients, warming and changes in mixing make plankton blooms grow or shrink, especially in estuaries.
variables.caveat: Muddy coastal water can confuse the algorithm; values are often analysed on a log scale.

variables.name: Cloud fraction
variables.plain_definition: The share of the sky covered by cloud, from 0 (clear) to 1 (overcast).
variables.why_trends: Clouds respond to warming and pollution, and they control how much sunlight reaches the ground.
variables.caveat: Daytime only (Aqua overpass about 13:30 local time).

region_presets.name: Indo-Gangetic Plain, India
region_presets.why: Dense farming and cities; winter haze and crop-residue burning.

region_presets.name: Tamil Nadu region, India
region_presets.why: Gets most rain from the October-December monsoon, unlike north India.

region_presets.name: Delhi National Capital Region
region_presets.why: One of the world's largest cities; haze and NO2 hotspot.

region_presets.name: Los Angeles basin, USA
region_presets.why: Emissions rules have cut NO2 for decades: a contrast with fast-growing cities.

region_presets.name: Southern Amazon 'arc of deforestation', Brazil
region_presets.why: Forest clearing and fire change greenness, land temperature and smoke.

region_presets.name: Central Sahel, Africa
region_presets.why: Rainfall recovered after the 1980s droughts; greening and dust are debated.

region_presets.name: Ganges-Brahmaputra delta and Sundarbans
region_presets.why: Tidal estuary with mangroves, river sediment and plankton blooms.

region_presets.name: Chesapeake Bay, USA
region_presets.why: A well-studied estuary: chlorophyll and water temperature trends.

region_presets.name: Western Himalaya
region_presets.why: Snow and glaciers feed the Indus and Ganges.

region_presets.name: Northwest India aquifer (Punjab-Haryana-Rajasthan)
region_presets.why: GRACE showed fast groundwater loss from irrigation pumping.

region_presets.name: Central equatorial Pacific (Nino 3.4)
region_presets.why: El Nino region: strong natural ups and downs that can hide or mimic trends.
